summary: The shared building blocks of the UI: severity, status and score badges, chips, panels, empty/loading/error states, the segmented control with its sliding pill, a syntax-coloured JSON block and a tiny safe markdown renderer. Every helper returns output from dom.js's auto-escaping `html` template (or `raw` for markup it built and escaped itself), so pages can combine them freely without XSS risk. The pages, the charts and the detail drawers in details.js all import from here.

notes.text: File header. Every helper here returns `html` or `raw` output (a `SafeHTML` object from dom.js), so a page can drop the result into another `html` template without it being escaped twice and without opening an XSS hole.

Imports from dom.js: `LEVELS` (the ordered list LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL), the `fmt` formatters, the auto-escaping `html` template, `levelOf` (score to level at the 30/60/80 thresholds) and `raw` (marks trusted markup).
Imports `movePill` from the motion wrapper. It slides the highlight 'pill' of a segmented control under the pressed button.
Imports the SVG icon builder and the event-type-to-icon map from icons.js.
Doc comment stating the accessibility rule: severity is shown three ways (colour, a 4-pip signal bar and the level word), so it still reads correctly for colour-blind users or in greyscale.
`sev(level)` builds a severity badge. `LEVELS.indexOf(level) + 1` turns the level into how many pips to light: LOW 1, MEDIUM 2, HIGH 3, CRITICAL 4 (an unknown level gives -1 + 1 = 0, so none).

Creates four small `i` elements and adds the class `on` to the first `lit` of them. components.css gives the pips rising heights (5, 7, 9 and 11px, like a phone's signal bar) and dims unlit ones to 25% opacity; `raw` is safe here because the markup is fixed and contains no data.

Returns the badge. The `lvl-${level}` class sets the `--lvl` colour variables that tint it, followed by the pips and the level word itself, so the number of lit bars and the text carry the meaning even without colour.
Closes `sev()`.
`status(value)` renders an incident status (OPEN, INVESTIGATING or RESOLVED). CSS draws a dot before the text, the value doubles as a class that colours it, and the word itself is always printed too.

`score(value, level)` renders a risk score as a number plus a 44px mini bar. The level defaults to `levelOf(value)`, and because scores run from 0 to 100 the score is used directly as the bar's width percentage.
Closes `score()`.
`signalChips(signals, max)` shows signal names as chips, at most `max` of them (default 3). An empty list shows a faint 'none' rather than an empty table cell.
Takes the first `max` signals and wraps each in a chip; `html` escapes the signal text.
Outputs the chips plus, when there were more than `max`, an overflow chip such as '+2', which keeps table rows compact.
Closes `signalChips()`.

`mitre(m)` renders a MITRE ATT&CK technique (for example T1110.001) as a small link to attack.mitre.org, with the technique name as a hover title. `target="_blank"` opens a new tab, `rel="noopener"` stops that tab from reaching back into this one, and a signal with no mapping returns an empty string.

`avatar(name, large)` shows a customer's initials in a rounded square (`fmt.initials` takes the first letters of up to two words). It is `aria-hidden` because the full name is always printed beside it; `large` adds the bigger `lg` size used in drawers.
`eventIcon(type, size)` picks the icon for an event type from `EVENT_ICONS`, falling back to the generic `activity` icon for an unknown type.

`panel({...})` builds the standard dashboard card. All options are named and all except `title` have defaults, so a page passes only what it needs: the `title`, an optional `idx` number, `tools` for the header's right side, the `body`, extra classes or an `id`.
Opens the `section` with any extra classes. (An `id` option that no page used was removed; it was also built with `raw()`, an unescaped HTML sink.)
The header row: an optional small index label (like '01'), the `h3` title, and a `tools` slot that CSS pushes to the right edge for buttons, tags or a segmented control.
The body wrapper, with optional extra classes such as `flush` for edge-to-edge tables.
Closes the section, the template literal and the function.
`empty(text, iconName)` is the standard empty state: a 22px icon (default `layers`) above a short message, used when a list or chart has nothing to show.

`skeleton(rows, height)` draws grey placeholder bars while data loads. Each bar's width cycles through 92%, 78% and 64% (`92 - (i % 3) * 14`) so it looks like ragged lines of text, and the `skeleton` class adds a moving shimmer in CSS.
`errorBox(message)` shows a red error panel with an alert icon. The message is escaped by `html`, so error text from the server cannot inject markup.
Doc comment: `seg()` only produces markup; behaviour is attached later with `bindSeg` once the HTML is in the page.

`seg(name, options, value)` renders a segmented control, a row of mutually exclusive buttons. `name` identifies it, `options` is a list of `[value, label]` pairs and `value` is the option selected initially.

The container gets `role="group"` and a `data-seg` attribute so `bindSeg` can find it. Its first child is the empty `pill` span: CSS places it absolutely behind the buttons (z-index 0 versus 1), and it is the highlight that slides from option to option.

One `button` per option. `type="button"` stops it from submitting a surrounding form, and `aria-pressed` (the string 'true' or 'false') tells both assistive technology and the CSS which option is active. Line 52 closes `seg()`.
`bindSeg(root, name, onChange)` brings a mounted segmented control to life. `onChange` is called with the newly selected value.
Finds the control inside `root` by its `data-seg` name, and returns `null` instead of throwing if it isn't there.

Places the pill for the first time on the next animation frame (just before the browser paints), after the rest of the current rendering code has run. `movePill` reads the pressed button's `offsetLeft` and `offsetWidth` and snaps the pill there without animation (`instant = true`).

`select()` presses one button and releases the others (`aria-pressed` is the standard way to mark a toggle button for assistive technology), then animates the pill over to it with a spring, or moves it instantly when motion is off.
A single click listener on the whole control handles every button (event delegation). It is `async` because it may wait for the caller's work.
Finds the clicked button. Clicks between buttons, or on the option that is already active, are ignored, so `onChange` only fires for a real change.
Remembers the option pressed before, then presses the clicked one straight away, so the control feels instant.

Hands the new value (the button's `data-value`, always a string) to the caller. A caller whose work can fail, like the incident drawer's status save, returns `false` on failure and the control goes back to the previous option. It used to keep showing a status that was never saved, and ignored a second click on it.
Closes the click handler.
Returns the control's element for callers that want it, and closes `bindSeg()`.

One module-level listener: when the window is resized, responsive layout can change the buttons' sizes, so every segmented control on the page re-snaps its pill instantly. It is registered once, when this module first loads.
Doc comment for `jsonBlock`: the JSON text is HTML-escaped first, and only then are colour spans wrapped around its tokens.

`jsonBlock(value)` turns any value into a syntax-coloured code block (the Raw record in the event drawer and the API console use it). `JSON.stringify(value, null, 2)` produces pretty-printed text indented by two spaces.

Escapes the three characters that matter inside an HTML element. `&` goes first so the entities created by the next two replacements aren't escaped again; quotes can stay as they are because the text becomes element content, not an attribute.

One regular expression finds every token, with a capture group for each kind: a quoted string (escaped characters allowed) optionally followed by a colon, the words `true`, `false` or `null`, or a number with optional decimals and exponent. The scan runs left to right, so digits inside a string are consumed with the string and never coloured on their own.
A string followed by a colon is an object key: it gets class `k` and the colon gets class `p` (punctuation). Any other string is a value and gets class `s`.
Booleans and `null` get class `b`.
Whatever else matched must be a number, class `n`. The colours for `k`, `s`, `b`, `n` and `p` are defined in components.css.
Closes the replacement callback and the chain of `.replace` calls.
Returns the result in a `pre` element with class `code`, which keeps the indentation. It is wrapped in `raw` because escaping was already done by hand on line 72; line 79 closes the function.
Doc comment: a deliberately tiny, safe markdown renderer (used for the AI Analyst's answers). Everything is escaped first, then only bold text, inline code and dash bullets are allowed.

`markdown(text)` converts the input to a string (`?? ""` turns `null` or `undefined` into an empty string) and escapes `&`, `<` and `>`. From this point on, any HTML in the text, even HTML an AI model produced, is just harmless characters.

`inline()` formats text within a line: a phrase wrapped in double asterisks becomes bold, and a phrase wrapped in backticks becomes inline code. Together with the list, paragraph and ref-button markup below, these are the only tags the renderer ever creates.

Turns record IDs (INC- plus 4 digits, EVT- plus 5, USR- plus 4) into small `ref` buttons carrying the ID in `data-ref`. A document-wide click handler in main.js passes them to `openRef`, so an incident mentioned in an answer opens its drawer when clicked.
Splits the escaped text into blocks at blank lines (two or more newlines in a row), then splits each block into its lines.
If every line in a block starts with '- ', the whole block becomes a bulleted list: each line, minus its first two characters, goes through `inline()` into a list item.
Otherwise finds the first line that starts with '- ' (or -1 when there is none).

When bullets begin part-way through a block (index above 0), the lines before them become one paragraph joined with line breaks, and every line from the first bullet onwards becomes a list item, with the leading '- ' stripped where present.
A block without bullets becomes a single paragraph, keeping its line breaks as `br` elements.

Closes the block mapping, then joins the blocks and returns them as `raw` HTML. That is safe because the only markup in the string is what this function inserted after escaping; line 97 closes `markdown()`.
